Here's What It Takes On Average To Ship a 13-Foot Camper to the US From Around the World
9 photos
Photo: Niewiadów
I was recently looking for some of the world’s lightest and most affordable campers, with Australia under the looking glass. It’s here that I ran across something that was to be expected: a brand selling a camper that’s designed, built, and used heavily on another continent.
Seeing campers being sold overseas in nations where they didn’t see their birth is nothing new, but what most people don’t understand is that, to sell a camper outside of the country where it was initially conceived comes with some drawbacks, one of the primary being that cost is almost always higher than if they were being sold on their maternal grounds.
Photo: Niewiadów As mentioned, all this started off with the camper before use, which in Australia is marketed and sold as the Euro Glider but which is in fact a variation of a Niewiadów N126, a camper which, on its native continent, sells for around €8,500, or roughly US$9,400. This means around AU$14,000, all this at exchange rates at the time of publishing.
However, the N126 series is currently up for grabs at around AU$36,000 through some dealers in Australia, so over double the price of the initial unit. Sure, some profit for the team selling it is to be accounted for, and some upgrades, although the unit does come across as one of the most basic out there, leaving us with a rather high “premium.”
Jumps in prices are primarily the result of one very important stage in bringing an import to your doorstep, just that, bringing it over to you, which means “ delivery fees .” You have to be unaware of how the world works to think that you can just bring an RV over to the US from another country and not have to pay a premium for it.
Photo: Niewiadów That said, I’ve decided to do a bit of research and find out what it can cost you to bring a simple travel trailer over to the US from various continents, so that you can have an idea of what to expect if you ever run into an import RV and want to make it your own but it isn’t already sold locally.
To make things easier to understand, we can continue to have the Niewiadów N126 in the spotlight, a camper born over in Poland. It’s comes in with a GVWR of 750 kg (1,653 lbs), occupies a space that’s almost 4 m (13 ft) long, 2 m (6.5 ft) wide, and 2,2 m (7.3 ft) tall.
According to sources, it’ll depend a whole lot on the method of shipping and the size of the package. Since we already know the dimensions, we can start with FCL of container shipping. For a 20-ft container (smallest option), we need on average of $4,500 to get things rolling right out of Poland.
Photo: Ian Taylor If you’re looking for a cheaper route, you can opt for a Roll-on and Roll-off (Ro-Ro) method which may save you around $1,500 but stores the camper below deck and exposes it to rough port handling. The issue here is that you will need to make sure the camper leaves from a port that can handle this method, and for the N126, you have to head over to Germany to do so.
This means extra cash dropped on getting the camper there in the first place, so you might as well opt for container shipping anyway.
Now there are several countries that produce campers which Americans are sure to want to get their hands on, and so so, I’ve put together a list of nations from where we can import a Niewiadów N126-sized camper. Keep in mind that these are averages and shipping rates do differ from one company to the next.
Australia FCL: $4,800 Ro-Ro: $3,000 China FCL: $4,500 Ro-Ro: $5,000 South Africa FCL: $2,500 Ro-Ro: $2,500 India FCL: $3,500 Ro-Ro: $3,500 Italy FCL: $3,500 Ro-Ro: $2,500 Germany 20FCL: $3,500 Ro-Ro: $3,500 UK FCL: $2,500 Ro-Ro: $2,000
Now, these are just a couple nations that we can typically import from and again, just some averages that I scrounged up. Sometimes, prices do exceed what I’ve jotted down and sometimes, even fall below those numbers.
Some of the countries on our list here are also nations from which American dealers already import campers or the brands themselves are selling units on US soil. Australia is one of them and so is Italy. China also makes the list, but they make the list for just about any nation in the world and quite heavily in Australia.
Photo: Ali Mkumbwa If you find an Australian, Italian, Chinese, or camper from any other nation other than the US, you understand why the usual premium pricing.
However, this is not all importing a camper entails, with fees like port handling falling into the bill you’ll need to cover, along with customs fees, DOT fees, some of which can will blow your mind, and again, the size of the unit you’re shipping will greatly impact how much you pay for one. Fees, fees, fees.
That said, while our example of the Niewiadów N126 being sold in Australia at over double it’s price may sound farfetched, this little example of what it can take to import a unit should tell you a bit about why we’re always paying extra for imported goods, not just campers. Then there’s Trump, but that’s a story for another day.
PS Keep in mind that these rates apply to campers that fit in a 20-foot container and sources mention that shipping companies calculate rates based on volume and weight and bill you for whichever results in the highest price for the service.
